title: Gethsemane (Luke 22:39–46)
hook: in a garden at night he prays, sweating, not my will but yours

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last supper, bread and a cup, and your line: remember me. Who did you remember at the table? After the meal, they sing, and walk out into the dark. Day sixty-six.

The night before surgery. The night before a hard goodbye. Lying awake, bargaining with the ceiling. Across the brook Cedron from Jerusalem rises the Mount of Olives, and late this night Jesus goes there, Luke says, as he often did, and his disciples follow. Matthew and Mark name the place: Gethsemane. John calls it a garden. Tradition says the name means oil press, where olives are crushed. Tonight he's the one being pressed. Today's word: Gethsemane.
screen: `THE NIGHT BEFORE THE DREADED THING.` → `THE MOUNT OF OLIVES, LATE.` → `GETHSEMANE: THE OIL PRESS.`

segments.voice: He tells his friends to pray that they don't fall into testing. Then he goes a stone's throw away, kneels, and prays, in the King James Bible: "Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done." Notice what he asks first. Take it away. He doesn't pretend he wants to suffer. He asks, honestly, for another way. In Isaiah and Jeremiah, a cup can stand for suffering and judgment. And only then: nevertheless. That word again, the one Simon said over his empty nets. Not my will, but yours. In Mark he calls God Abba, the family word for father. Then Luke gives a detail: "And being in an agony he prayed more earnestly: and his sweat was as it were great drops of blood falling down to the ground." As it were. Like drops of blood. Luke may mean his sweat fell heavy as blood, or that it was mixed with blood; readers have taken it both ways. And a small honesty: some readers point out that these verses, with the angel who comes to strengthen him, are not in every early copy of Luke. Agony is Luke's Greek word, agonia, a word also used for the strain of a contest, a wrestler's or a runner's. And his friends? He comes back and finds them asleep, Luke says, sleeping for sorrow. He wakes them with a question: "Why sleep ye? rise and pray, lest ye enter into temptation." The shape of the prayer is plain: say what you want, all of it, and then, nevertheless.
screen: `REMOVE THIS CUP FROM ME.` · `NEVERTHELESS, NOT MY WILL.` · `AGONIA: A WRESTLER'S STRAIN.` · `SLEEPING FOR SORROW.` · then, large: `NOT MY WILL, BUT THINE, BE DONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let yourself get still. Think of the hardest thing in front of you right now. Something you'd take away if you could. Don't dress it up. In your own words, silently, say what you really want. All of it. Take it away, or make it different, or let me off. Then, if you can, notice what it would be like to hold it a little more loosely. You don't have to get to nevertheless today. If you pray, you can pray it to God just as honestly. The bell holds the time.
Gethsemane. A garden whose name, tradition says, means oil press, where he prayed take this cup away, and then, not my will.
Your line: not my will. Today, when something doesn't go your way, say what you wanted honestly first, then see if you can loosen your grip, even a little. Day sixty-six.

howItsDone: Many churches keep a watch on the night of Maundy Thursday, staying up to pray in memory of Gethsemane, and some Christians keep a holy hour of prayer on other nights. Pilgrims to Jerusalem visit an olive garden on the Mount of Olives with very old trees.

original.note: Greek: agony, the strain of a wrestler or runner in the contest. Luke's word for Jesus in the garden.

trapdoor: what you thought: a quiet prayer in a garden before the arrest.
what it means: he asks honestly for another way, and then lets go: not my will, but yours.

what a scholar hears: tradition reads Gethsemane as oil press, agonia was also used of an athlete's struggle, and Luke 22:43–44, the angel and the sweat like blood, is absent from some early copies of Luke.

notes: Luke 22:43–44 is absent from several early manuscripts (e.g., P75, Codex Vaticanus) and present in others (e.g., Codex Sinaiticus original hand, Bezae); stated plainly and neutrally.
The script does not claim hematidrosis; it gives both readings of 'as it were'.
'They sing' in the review: Mark 14:26 / Matthew 26:30 ('when they had sung an hymn').

The practice invites honest, unscripted prayer in the listener's own words; no prayer text is written. The index practice reads 'pray the hardest honest prayer you have'; phrased as an invitation for those who pray.
Maundy Thursday watch (altar of repose) and holy hour in howItsDone; confirm.

Fresh review (days 57–74): hook drops the banned 'Think of' opener and the unsourced 'olive grove'; the place is now sourced to John 18:1 (brook Cedron, a garden) and the 'oil press' meaning is given as tradition. 'Nevertheless' now points clearly to Simon at the empty nets (day 50, Luke 5:5), not the walk on water. Cut 'stayed with readers for centuries' and 'the prayer many Christians find the most honest in the Bible'; the manuscript note is softened to 'not in every early copy'.
